The move display identifies the most recently recognized action and its directional variant within 100 milliseconds of the input being accepted.
The move display records whether the action connected with the dummy, was guarded, whiffed, or was interrupted.
The player remains in Training Mode after attacks, knockback, or hazard interactions; no round win, loss, or best-of-three transition occurs.

scenarios.title: Use a stationary dummy and reset the drill
given: Training Mode is active with the stationary dummy selected.
The fighter, dummy, and arena have non-default positions or combat states.
The dummy has been hit, moved by knockback, or placed into hit-stun.
when: The player activates Reset Training using the configured reset control.
The player attacks the stationary dummy again after the reset completes.
then: The fighter returns to the configured player start position and the dummy returns to the configured dummy start position in the selected depth lanes.
Fighter and dummy health, hit-stun, knockback, guard state, active attack state, momentum, and recovery state return to their training defaults.
The current, hazard telegraph, hazard active window, and arena interaction state return to the same deterministic starting phase on every reset.
The move display history is cleared and the next accepted action becomes the first displayed action.
The dummy remains stationary until the player changes its mode or directly interacts with it.

scenarios.title: Practice against a repeatable dummy pattern
given: Training Mode is active and the repeatable dummy mode is selected.
A deterministic dummy pattern containing movement, guard, and attack actions is loaded.
The fighter and dummy are at their configured training start positions.
when: The player starts the repeatable dummy pattern.
The pattern reaches its final action or the player activates Reset Training.
then: The dummy performs the same recorded pattern with the same timing and lane transitions on every run.
The pattern pauses or restarts at its defined beginning when the player activates Reset Training.
The move display identifies both player actions and dummy actions, including whether a player attack hit, was guarded, or missed.
The repeatable dummy pattern does not create a round result, alter best-of-three scores, or persist changes outside the current training session.

scenarios.title: Reset while the hazard is active
given: Training Mode is active and the arena hazard is in its telegraphed or active phase.
The fighter or dummy is currently affected by the hazard, in hit-stun, or in knockback.
when: The player activates Reset Training during the hazard telegraph, active window, hit-stun, or knockback.
then: The reset completes at the next simulation-safe frame without applying additional hazard damage, knockback, or hit-stun.
Both combatants return to their configured training positions and health.
The hazard returns to its deterministic initial phase and its telegraph is not left visually active after reset.
No hazard hit, attack result, or move-display entry is generated solely by the reset operation.

scenarios.title: Continue training when a controller disconnects
given: Training Mode is active with a local controller assigned to the player.
The player is not in a round transition or loading screen.
when: The assigned controller disconnects or stops reporting input.
then: The fighter stops receiving movement and attack input within 100 milliseconds of the last valid input sample.
The game pauses training and identifies the disconnected controller using the existing pause/input-reconnect flow.
No buffered input causes an attack, dash, lane change, or reset while the controller is disconnected.
After the controller is reconnected and the player confirms resume, the training state is preserved unless the player explicitly chooses Reset Training.

scenarios.title: Reset at the start and end of an input frame
given: Training Mode is active at 60 simulation updates per second.
The player activates Reset Training while an input frame contains a movement, attack, hazard, or rebound event.
when: The reset request is received before the frame is simulated or after the frame has completed.
then: The reset is applied exactly once at a simulation-safe boundary.
No partially applied attack, rebound, current displacement, hazard effect, or duplicate reset remains after the reset.
The resulting state is identical for equivalent reset requests regardless of whether the request arrived before or after the frame simulation boundary.

assetMetadata.name: Aqua Fighter Default Input Control Layout
assetMetadata.purpose: Defines the default gamepad and keyboard mappings for movement, attacks, techniques, dash, guard, menus, and training controls.
acceptanceCriteria: Gamepad and keyboard defaults match the controls specified in GDD section 2.2.
Every gameplay action can be remapped independently.
Keyboard rollover validation is available for all mapped gameplay actions.
Controller dead-zone configuration is persisted per profile.
Input mappings serialize deterministically for replay and online simulation.

assetMetadata.name: Deterministic Input Buffer and Direction Sampler
assetMetadata.purpose: Captures movement intent, attack direction, buffered chain inputs, dash buffers, and serialized input timing for deterministic gameplay and replay.
acceptanceCriteria: Offline input sampling runs at 240 Hz.
Offline gameplay simulation runs at 120 Hz and online simulation runs at fixed 60 Hz.
Attack direction is stored at attack commitment and is unaffected by later analog noise unless steering is explicitly enabled.
The 100 ms dash buffer and 100 ms attack-chain buffer are represented consistently across simulation rates.
Identical serialized inputs produce identical movement and attack outcomes across supported platforms.

assetMetadata.name: Aqua Fighter Combat State Machine
assetMetadata.purpose: Controls fighter states including neutral movement, attacks, guard, hit-stun, launch, knockdown, rebound, hazard stun, and recovery states.
acceptanceCriteria: The state machine distinguishes light hit-stun, heavy hit-stun, launch, knockdown, rebound, and hazard stun.
Movement and attack input are suppressed or permitted according to the active state definition.
All state transitions are deterministic and serializable for replay.
Guard break produces a guaranteed minimum vulnerability window.
Recovery options are limited by the configured resource, cooldown, or move-specific rule.
sourceReferences: GDD 2.5 Guard, Guard Break, Hit-Stun, and Recovery Options

assetMetadata.name: Fighter Combat Data Schema
assetMetadata.purpose: Stores deterministic fighter attributes, attack definitions, movement tuning, signature mechanics, weaknesses, defensive options, and arena interaction profiles.
acceptanceCriteria: The schema supports twelve launch fighter entries.
Each fighter entry contains a readable silhouette reference, movement accent, universal attack set, signature mechanic, weakness, approach tool, defensive answer, and arena interaction profile.
Attack startup, active, recovery, damage, hit-stun, knockback, guard interaction, and cancel windows are data-driven.
All authoritative numeric fields use deterministic integer or fixed-point representations.
Invalid or incomplete fighter data fails validation before entering a playable build.

assetMetadata.name: Universal Attack and Hurt Volume Library
assetMetadata.purpose: Provides authored hit volumes, hurt volumes, guard volumes, lane tolerances, and collision labels for readable fighter interactions.
acceptanceCriteria: The library contains neutral light, heavy, rising, descending, dash, and follow-up attack volume definitions.
Every active attack volume has an associated damage, hit-stun, knockback, lane tolerance, and guard interaction value.
Volumes are visualized in training mode at gameplay scale.
Collision results are identical for identical positions, states, and inputs.
Volume placement does not conceal the attacking pose, defender reaction, or knockback direction.
sourceReferences: GDD 3.2 Movement Plane and Depth Lanes

assetMetadata.name: Deterministic Damage and Combo Scaling Rules
assetMetadata.purpose: Calculates damage, combo scaling, counter-hit modifiers, guard modifiers, environmental multipliers, and technique resource modifiers.
acceptanceCriteria: The default scaling values are 100 percent for the first hit, 92 percent for the second, 84 percent for the third, and a minimum of 45 percent thereafter.
Environmental hit multipliers use a separately capped value.
Damage outcomes are deterministic and independent of platform floating-point behavior.
Guard, counter-hit, technique resource, and mode-specific modifiers are individually auditable in combat logs.
The system prevents infinite or low-risk damage loops through configured route and scaling limits.

assetMetadata.name: Aquatic Technique Data Schema
assetMetadata.purpose: Defines character techniques, including timing, damage, resource cost, cooldown, direction, guard behavior, environmental interaction, telegraph, counterplay, and deterministic simulation rules.
acceptanceCriteria: Each technique record contains startup, active frames, recovery, damage, hit-stun, knockback, resource cost, cooldown, directional behavior, guard interaction, environmental interaction, telegraph, counterplay, VFX reference, and audio reference.
The schema supports direct damage, space control, current creation, momentum redirection, defensive escape, cover denial, combo routing, hazard interruption, and resource conversion techniques.
Every technique has an explicit online determinism flag and serialized execution parameters.
Missing counterplay or telegraph data prevents the technique from being marked production-ready.

assetMetadata.name: Deterministic Arena Collision Resolution System
assetMetadata.purpose: Resolves movement, current force, dash and technique displacement, knockback, rebound, arena boundaries, wreckage, and reef contacts in a fixed priority order.
acceptanceCriteria: Collision processing follows the specified nine-step priority order from player movement through reef contact resolution.
The system uses authored static shapes and deterministic slide, snap, unsticking, and boundary rules.
No collision result depends on emergent rigid-body restitution.
Identical replay inputs produce identical collision positions and state transitions.
Fighters cannot be trapped indefinitely by wreckage corners or authored cover.

assetMetadata.name: Three-Lane Underwater Arena Collision Data
assetMetadata.purpose: Defines the 2D combat plane, foreground, center, and background gameplay lanes, lane transitions, arena boundaries, cover shapes, reef contacts, and hazard occupancy.

scopeReviewContent.critique: Twelve fighters multiplied by unique movement accents, signature mechanics, techniques, animations, VFX, balance data, arena interactions, tutorials, and matchup testing is a major production burden. The roster also creates a large balance matrix before the core combat is proven.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Cut V1 to 4 fighters: one balanced tutorial fighter, one mobility specialist, one control specialist, and one heavy fighter. Build all four from the same universal base kit and allow only one signature mechanic per fighter. Add the remaining roster only after the combat prototype survives external playtesting.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: A smaller roster preserves the identity of character-driven combat while making animation, balance, readability, and QA achievable for a 1–5 person team. Four fighters are enough to validate whether the game has real matchup depth.

scopeReviewContent.critique: Deterministic simulation, rollback or lockstep networking, input delay handling, desync detection, matchmaking, reconnect behavior, region support, ranking, moderation, and platform certification are separate products inside the game. Supporting 240 Hz input, 120 Hz offline simulation, and 60 Hz online simulation increases synchronization risk.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Remove online ranked play from V1. Ship local versus, training, and possibly same-device challenge modes first. If online is mandatory, target one fixed 60 Hz simulation with rollback and no ranked ladder, crossplay, or reconnect complexity until the core combat is validated.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: Online infrastructure can consume the entire project and still fail to make the combat feel good. Local play proves the hook more cheaply and exposes balance problems before networking multiplies them.

scopeReviewContent.feature: Multiple simulation rates and deterministic replay
scopeReviewContent.critique: Maintaining 240 Hz input sampling, 120 Hz offline simulation, 60 Hz online simulation, fixed-point movement, serialized timing markers, replay validation, and platform-independent outcomes is a high-risk engineering requirement. Differences in rounding, input buffering, collision order, and animation timing will create difficult-to-reproduce bugs.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Use one fixed simulation rate for V1, preferably 60 Hz or 120 Hz depending on prototype feel. Store inputs and deterministic random seeds only after the simulation is stable. Defer authoritative replay verification and cross-rate compatibility.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: One clock dramatically reduces debugging and QA cost. The movement hook can still be preserved without building a custom deterministic technology stack before the design has been proven.

scopeReviewContent.critique: Currents, reefs, wreckage, cover, lane splitting, rebounds, projectiles, hazards, hit-stun, knockback, and techniques all interacting creates a combinatorial collision matrix. Every combination needs rules for priority, escape, camera visibility, corner behavior, and competitive fairness.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Choose one signature environmental interaction for V1: authored currents plus simple boundary rebounds. Remove hard cover, movable-looking wreckage, lane-splitting objects, and complex environmental multipliers. Use static visual props until the core interaction is proven.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: The underwater setting remains mechanically meaningful, but the team avoids implementing several overlapping physics systems simultaneously. A single strong environmental verb is more memorable than five inconsistent ones.

scopeReviewContent.critique: Depth lanes require lane-aware hitboxes, attack tolerance, transitions, camera composition, cover rules, projectile behavior, collision handling, player readability, and edge-case testing during hit-stun and knockback. They can also make attacks feel like they miss for unclear reasons.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Prototype two lanes first, or make depth a single short dodge/shift action rather than a continuously available three-lane system. Restrict attacks to clear lane rules and avoid attacks that hit arbitrary lane combinations in V1.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: Two lanes can preserve the underwater positioning hook while reducing visual ambiguity and collision cases. The third lane should be earned only if testing shows it creates meaningful decisions rather than confusion.

scopeReviewContent.feature: Universal chain system plus fighter-specific branches
scopeReviewContent.critique: Buffered inputs, priority rules, duplicate rejection, route limits, branch-specific timing, cancel windows, hit-confirm behavior, animation transitions, and training feedback are more complex than a simple three-hit combo system. Ambiguous directional input will generate frequent player-facing errors.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Ship one universal Light-Light-Heavy chain and one directional finisher per fighter. Remove branching route trees, alternate chain priorities, and extensive fighter-specific cancel logic from V1.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: A small, reliable combo grammar provides immediate accessibility and enough timing depth to test the combat. Complexity can be added after input clarity and hit confirmation are proven.

scopeReviewContent.feature: Aquatic technique slots and environmental technique interactions
scopeReviewContent.critique: Each technique requires authored timing, hitboxes, resource behavior, guard rules, telegraphs, VFX, sound, animation, counterplay, and interaction testing with currents, cover, rebounds, hazards, and every fighter state. Supporting multiple technique roles per character creates substantial balance and content cost.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Give each fighter one signature technique in V1. Use a shared resource model and restrict techniques to one or two interaction categories, such as damage or movement control. Defer alternate techniques, modifiers, grabs, traps, clouds, and persistent hazards.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: One excellent ability per fighter protects character identity and keeps the balance surface manageable. It also makes the tutorial and control scheme much easier to understand.

scopeReviewContent.feature: Guard, guard strain, guard breaks, recovery options, and multiple defensive states
scopeReviewContent.critique: Manual guard, directional arcs, guard pushback, strain thresholds, repeated-pressure rules, guard breaks, air techs, dash recovery, technique cancels, reef rebounds, and lane escapes can create defensive complexity that is difficult to teach and balance. The design risks producing situations where players cannot tell which escape is valid.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Use one guard state, one clear guard-break rule, and one universal recovery option. Remove fighter-specific defensive exceptions and resource-based recovery variants from V1. Make guard direction either full-front with a clear facing indicator or omnidirectional.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: A focused defensive layer supports competitive mastery without requiring a state-machine encyclopedia. Fewer escape tools also make offense, punishment, and spectator readability stronger.

scopeReviewContent.critique: Every hazard needs telegraphs, activation timing, collision outcomes, interruption behavior, recovery rules, camera treatment, accessibility settings, and competitive balance. Hazard interactions with currents, knockback, guard, cover, and techniques will multiply QA requirements. Background creatures and spectacle can also be mistaken for gameplay threats.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Exclude hazards from ranked and standard V1 matches. Include one optional casual arena hazard with a fixed timer, obvious telegraph, fixed damage, and a guaranteed escape route. Treat background creatures as non-interactive visual dressing.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: The environmental fantasy survives in casual play without allowing random-feeling hazards to undermine competitive combat. This protects fairness while keeping the production and test matrix small.

scopeReviewContent.feature: Dynamic camera, anime spectacle, and impact presentation
scopeReviewContent.critique: Camera shake, hit-stop, speed lines, finishing poses, callouts, water effects, lane visibility, silhouettes, and readable hurt reactions compete for screen space. Effects that look good in isolation may obscure hit volumes, current telegraphs, or directional knockback. Camera behavior also becomes difficult around boundaries and cover.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Use a fixed camera with limited, globally tuned hit-stop and one restrained impact effect. Remove character-specific camera moves, finishing poses, large screen overlays, and complex speed-line packages from V1. Add an effects intensity accessibility slider.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: Readability is a pillar, not decoration. A restrained presentation is faster to tune, easier to test, and more likely to make the movement and hit confirmation feel deliberate.

scopeReviewContent.feature: Wreckage as hard cover and line-of-sight gameplay
scopeReviewContent.critique: Cover introduces occlusion, corner trapping, projectile path rules, lane-specific collision, minimum escape distances, camera conflicts, and potential stalling strategies. It is effectively a tactical level-design system layered onto a fighter.
scopeReviewContent.suggestion: Cut hard cover from V1. Replace it with visually distinct static reefs or soft boundary zones that provide a single predictable rebound interaction. Reintroduce cover only after matches demonstrate a need for line-of-sight play.
scopeReviewContent.reasoning: Cover is not required to prove fluid momentum combat and is likely to create the most frustrating environmental edge cases. Removing it improves match pace and spectator clarity.
